newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Ringgit hits 38-month low, seen staying weak.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ringgit hits 38-month low, seen staying weak.

text.p: The ringgit hit a 38-month low against the dollar on Friday, continuing its slide as the central Bank Negara Malaysia stayed out of the market.
Foreign exchange dealers said more downside was likely in the short term.
The ringgit fell to 2.6430 to a dollar, its weakest level since May 1994. By 1130 GMT, it was quoted at 2.6400/50.
Dollar/ringgit was trading below 2.6000 in the morning.
Dealers said currency movements were exaggerated by thin trading volume and wide spreads.
"We are seeing 50 and even 80 points spread. That's why it's moving up so fast," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore. "You can move the market with just a few (million) dollars."
He said the sharp rise sparked off "some panic dollar-covering by genuine buyers".
The ringgit has fallen about five percent this week as speculators found a fresh target after attacking the Thai baht and Philippine peso.
Dealers said the next target was 2.6500.

"I think 2.6000 will be the new base for dollar/ringgit," said another European bank dealer. "All the other currencies in the region are falling, including the Singapore dollar. So it's no surprise to see ringgit coming off."
Dealers said there was talk that funds would try to push the dollar/ringgit rate to 2.75/2.80.
They said the central Bank Negara was not seen in the market despite the dollar's climb beyond the 2.6000 mark. The bank was earlier said to have been holding the rate at that level.
Dealers said the ringgit's undertone remained bearish following a perceived change in stance by Malaysian authorities.
Acting Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Tuesday Malaysia would allow market forces to dictate the exchange rate.
The statement was interpreted to mean Bank Negara had given up its strategy of vigorously defending a particular level and was willing to tolerate further ringgit weakness.
The central bank earlier this month spent more than $1 billion to defend the ringgit from speculative attack.

On Friday, when asked by reporters why Bank Negara had continued to stay away from the foreign exchange market despite the ringgit's fall, Anwar said: "What makes you think that 2.60 is not reasonable?"
He added it could go to a four-year low, but when asked if he was serious, he said: "I'm smiling, that means I'm joking."
The ringgit was at around 2.78 to a dollar in early 1994.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
